column14: Full review — tier-driven. A Critical tier calls for the deepest level of work: OSINT sweep across corporate and executive channels, trust-centre and sub-processor review, validation of held attestations, contract and schedule review, and a direct vendor questionnaire. Depth followed from the assigned tier rather than from the volume of material the vendor had published.
column16: Primary source — LinkedIn post published by the vendor's Chief Executive on 04-02-2026, linkedin.com/posts/larkspur-ceo-ai-assist (retrieved 09-03-2026; screenshot retained, as executive posts may later be amended or withdrawn). The post announces an internally developed application, "Larkspur Assist", built by the vendor's own engineering team to support servicing staff. It reports an AI upskilling programme described as reaching more than 400 servicing agents, with staff encouraged to apply the tooling in daily casework. Most materially, it describes automation of service delivery through agents that "draft borrower correspondence, summarise call history and progress routine arrangements without human handoff", framed as a reduction in average handling time. Supporting source — vendor careers listing, "Applied AI Engineer — Servicing Automation", www.larkspurservicing.example/careers (retrieved 09-03-2026), referencing agent orchestration against live account data and call transcription pipelines. Negative finding — no trust centre, sub-processor register or AI policy page is published on the vendor domain; searches of the domain and of the UK companies register returned nothing further. Entries are recorded in the Evidence Log sheet with retrieval dates and screenshots.
column17: Three usages are indicated. First, an in-house application that summarises borrower records and call content for servicing staff, implying transcription of recorded calls. Second, generative drafting of borrower-facing correspondence. Third, agentic progression of routine payment arrangements described as running without human handoff. The extent of human review over borrower-facing output is undetermined from public material and is carried forward to the vendor questionnaire.
column18: None named — Inconclusive. The post refers to "leading foundation models" without identifying a provider. The absence of a published sub-processor register leaves the question unresolved from public sources. Model provider identity, hosting region and retention terms are raised directly with the vendor.
column20: Sensitive borrower data, including vulnerability disclosures and call audio, appears to be processed by an application that progresses servicing actions with limited human checkpoints. No model provider is identified, leaving onward data flows, retention and training use untraceable, and the contract in force carries no AI clauses. Evidence is drawn from the vendor's own Chief Executive and is treated as reliable on the fact of use, while the data flows remain inferred. Sole-source dependency limits the scope for tolerating the position pending clarification.
column21: Issue a targeted questionnaire within 15 business days covering model provider identity, hosting region, retention, training use of borrower data, call-audio handling, and human review over agent-generated correspondence. Register the vendor on the AI sub-processor inventory with an unresolved-provider flag. Raise AI clauses at the Q4 2026 contract review, addressing training restrictions, sub-processor change notification, human oversight thresholds, and rights to review attestations. Escalate to the Third-Party Risk Committee where confirmation is not received.
